demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette:
Samir, at seventy-eight, had spent a lifetime reading the subtle language of the earth. As an environmental scientist, he understood ecosystems, the delicate balance of cause and effect, the long, slow arc of consequence. But in the six months since the accident, his own internal landscape had become a foreign and hostile territory he could not map. The logic that had governed his life and work had shattered, leaving only a chaotic and repeating loop of a single afternoon.

It was his grandson’s fifth birthday party. The garden was filled with laughter, the scent of grilled kofta, and the bright, chaotic energy of children. Samir had felt a profound sense of contentment, a warmth that settled deep in his chest. His grandson, Omar, had run to him, arms outstretched for the "airplane" game they always played. Samir had lifted him high, spinning him in a wide, joyous circle. The boy’s squeals of delight were the purest sound in the world. It was a moment of perfect happiness, the kind he now understood to be a harbinger of disaster. He hadn't noticed at first how Omar's laughter had caught, how a wheezing sound had begun to thread through his gasps for air. By the time Samir slowed, the boy was limp, his breathing a horrifying, rasping struggle. In the ensuing panic, as Samir lowered him, Omar’s small body slipped from his grasp. The sickening thud of his head on the stone patio is a sound that lives in Samir’s ears, louder than any memory.

Now, that moment is not a memory but a recurring reality. When it comes for him, he is no longer in his quiet study or his lab; he is back in the garden, the sun too bright, the weight of his grandson in his arms, the sound of that desperate, ragged breathing filling the world. He feels the slip, the loss of control, the impact. It is happening right now. When his wife, Layla, asks him what’s wrong, he opens his mouth but no coherent story emerges. He knows the sequence of events, a litany of facts he could recite, but the words to describe the feeling—the specific alchemy of joy turning to horror, of his own loving hands becoming instruments of harm—simply do not exist for him. The experience feels both hyper-real and utterly impossible. He, Samir, a man who had built a life on care and precision, could not have done that. The story feels like a lie his mind is telling him, even as his body relives it every day.

The triggers are everywhere, insidious traps laid in the fabric of his life. At the university, where he still consults, a graduate student climbing a steep embankment to collect a soil sample began to breathe heavily. The sound—that same strained, rhythmic panting—paralyzed Samir. He felt a cold sweat prickle his skin and had to invent an excuse to return to the car, leaving the student confused. The very feeling of peace has become a threat. Sitting with Layla on their porch, a rare moment of quiet contentment might start to settle over him, and a surge of pure terror follows. He has come to believe that happiness is a state of dangerous vulnerability, the moment just before the universe exacts its price. He will stand up abruptly, needing to check the locks on the doors or find some urgent, meaningless task, shattering the calm before it can betray him again.

Worst of all is the loss of touch. When Layla, his wife of fifty-two years, reaches for his hand or tries to embrace him, he flinches away with an involuntary shudder. Her touch, once his greatest comfort, now feels like a spark near gunpowder. He sees his own hands as weapons, his affection as a catalyst for ruin. The physical distance between them has grown into a chasm, an ache that sits alongside the sharper pains of the memory. It was Layla who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him one evening standing in the hallway, staring at the photographs of his grandchildren, his face a mask of such profound anguish that she told him she could not bear to watch him disappear anymore. Samir came to therapy not with any real hope of feeling happy again—an idea that now terrifies him—but with a desperate, flickering wish to simply exist in the same room as the people he loves without being certain that he will somehow bring them to ruin.
